statement.p: (a) Suppose that we consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = 2 x^2. Find the limit in this case:
(b) Now consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = 3 x^2. Find the limit in this case:
(c) Note that the results from (a) and (b) indicate that f has no limit as (x,y)\to (0,0) (be sure you can explain why!).
To show this more generally, consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = m x^2, for arbitrary m. Find the limit in this case:

p.em: (Be sure that you can explain how this result also indicates that f has no limit as (x,y)\to(0,0).

static.solution:
f does not have a limit as (x,y) approaches (0,0).
(a) If (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = 2 x^2, then f(x,y) = f(x,2 x^2) = \frac{4x^{2}-2x^{2}}{x^{2}+2x^{2}} = \frac{2}{3}.
Therefore \lim_{x\to0} f(x,2 x^2) = \frac{2}{3}.
(b) Similarly, if (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = 3 x^2, then f(x,y) = f(x,3 x^2) = \frac{4x^{2}-3x^{2}}{x^{2}+3x^{2}} = \frac{1}{4},
and so \lim_{x\to0} f(x,3 x^2) = \frac{1}{4}.
Because we have two different values for these limits, we know that the function doesn't have a limit at (0,0). No matter how close we are to the origin, there will be points on f(x,y) that are close to \frac{2}{3} and points that are close to \frac{1}{4}, whereas for the limit to exist the function must get close to a single value.
(c) We can see this more generally by considering the limit as (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = m x^2. Then f(x,y) = f(x,m x^2) = \frac{4-m}{1+m}, so that \lim_{x\to0} f(x,m x^2) = \frac{4-m}{1+m}, and we see for every different value of m we will get a different limiting value for the function. Thus the function does not have a limit at (0,0).
